algorithms.summary: One vertex per surface-crossing cell, relaxed to smooth the mesh while constrained to stay inside its own cell. The first dual contouring method.
algorithms.eli5: Instead of cutting triangles inside every cube, put one single point in each cube the surface passes through, then tug each point towards where the surface really crosses. Join the points of neighbouring cubes into quads. Far fewer and much better-shaped polygons — at the cost of softening every corner.
algorithms.description: Where marching cubes places vertices on cube edges, surface nets places exactly one vertex inside each cube that the surface passes through, and connects vertices in neighbouring cubes to form quads — the dual arrangement. The vertex positions are then relaxed iteratively, each one pulled toward the average of its linked neighbours to smooth the mesh, but clamped so it can never leave its original cube. That constraint is what stops the smoothing from shrinking the model away. It produces far better-shaped triangles than marching cubes and no ambiguous cases, at the cost of rounding sharp features even harder.
algorithms.citation: Constrained Elastic Surface Nets: Generating Smooth Surfaces from Binary Segmented Data, MICCAI '98

algorithms.name: Efros–Leung non-parametric synthesis
algorithms.summary: Grow a texture one pixel at a time by finding places in the sample whose neighbourhood matches the one you have so far.
algorithms.eli5: You have a scrap of texture and want more of it. Take the next empty pixel on the edge of what you have built, look at the pixels already around it, and search the whole scrap for spots whose surroundings look like that. Copy one of those spots' centre pixels in. Repeat, one pixel at a time.
algorithms.description: For each unfilled pixel on the growing boundary, take the window of already-known neighbours, find every location in the sample whose corresponding window is within a tolerance of the best match, and copy the centre pixel from one of those at random. The randomness among near-equal matches is what stops it degenerating into a verbatim copy; the tolerance is the one dial, and setting it too tight produces exact repetition while too loose produces mush. Nothing is fitted or learned: the sample is the model, which is why the paper is the origin of the whole example-based family. Its weaknesses are also its legacy — it is O(sample size) per pixel and therefore very slow, and it can "grow garbage", locking into a region of the sample and repeating it, which is what patch-based and optimisation-based successors were built to avoid.
algorithms.citation: Efros & Leung, Texture synthesis by non-parametric sampling, ICCV 1999, 1033–1038

algorithms.name: 3D Morphable Model
algorithms.summary: PCA over registered 3D face scans, separating shape from texture. The basis of every parametric face system since.
algorithms.eli5: The same idea in three dimensions, with scanned heads instead of photographs. Line every scan up so the tip of each nose is the same point, average them, and find the main ways they vary. Now a slider means something real — rounder, longer, older — and every setting is still a head a person could have.
algorithms.description: Take a set of 3D face scans and put them in dense correspondence, so that vertex n means the same anatomical point on every face — that registration step is most of the work, and it is what makes the linear algebra meaningful. Then run PCA separately over shape and over texture, giving two independent parameter spaces. New faces are linear combinations of the principal components, and because shape and texture are separated you can vary skin independently of bone structure. The paper also showed the inverse direction: fit the model's parameters by analysis-by-synthesis until the rendered face matches a photograph, recovering a 3D face from a single image. That fitting idea is the ancestor of modern photo-to-avatar pipelines, and the model's descendants — Basel, FLAME, SMPL for bodies — are the same construction with better data.
algorithms.citation: Blanz & Vetter, A morphable model for the synthesis of 3D faces, SIGGRAPH '99, 187–194

algorithms.name: Stable fluids
algorithms.summary: An unconditionally stable Navier–Stokes solver that never blows up regardless of timestep. Made real-time smoke practical.
algorithms.eli5: Smoke simulations used to explode the moment you took a big time step. The fix: instead of asking where each puff of smoke goes next, ask where each grid cell's smoke must have come *from*, and go and fetch it. Fetching can never overshoot, so it can never explode — you only lose a little swirl.
algorithms.description: Explicit fluid solvers explode if the timestep is too large relative to the grid — the CFL condition — which made interactive fluid impossible. Stam's method splits each step into stages that are each unconditionally stable: advection is done by semi-Lagrangian backtracing, tracing backwards from each grid cell to find where its contents came from and interpolating there, which can never produce a value outside the existing range and therefore cannot diverge; diffusion and pressure projection are solved implicitly as linear systems. The price is numerical dissipation — semi-Lagrangian advection smooths the field every step, so vorticity fades and smoke looks too smooth, which is why vorticity confinement was invented to add the lost swirl back. It is the paper that put fluid into games.
algorithms.citation: Stam, Stable Fluids, SIGGRAPH '99, 121–128

algorithms.name: Portilla–Simoncelli statistics matching
algorithms.summary: Measure a fixed set of statistics from the sample, then force noise to have the same ones. Nothing is copied.
algorithms.eli5: Instead of copying bits of the sample, measure it: how much of each size and direction of detail is present, and how those amounts relate to each other. Then take pure static and repeatedly nudge it until its measurements match. What comes out shares the sample's character without containing any piece of it.
algorithms.description: Decompose the sample with a steerable pyramid — a set of filters at several scales and orientations — and record a specific vocabulary of statistics: marginal moments of each band, correlations between neighbouring coefficients within a band, and correlations across scales and across orientations. Then start from white noise and alternately project it towards satisfying each statistic in turn until it converges. Because nothing is copied, the output cannot contain a fragment of the input, which matters for licensing and for scale: the model is a few thousand numbers regardless of how big the sample was. The paper is also the strongest statement of what a texture *is* — it identifies the minimal set of statistics whose match is perceptually sufficient — and that framing is what the neural style-transfer literature later rediscovered by replacing the steerable pyramid with a trained network and the hand-chosen statistics with Gram matrices.
algorithms.citation: Portilla & Simoncelli, A parametric texture model based on joint statistics of complex wavelet coefficients, International Journal of Computer Vision 40(1), 49–70

algorithms.name: Shuffle bags and pity timers
algorithms.authors: Game development practice; no single origin
algorithms.summary: Reshape a random distribution so it feels fair. Draw without replacement, or raise the odds after each failure.
algorithms.eli5: Real randomness feels unfair — it will happily hand you the same item five times running. So put one of each item in a bag, draw without putting them back, and refill only when it is empty. Now you get all of them, in a random order. A pity timer is the same idea for rare drops: quietly raise the odds every time you miss.
algorithms.description: Uniform random produces streaks, and players experience streaks as broken rather than random. Two standard corrections. A shuffle bag holds one token per possible outcome, draws without replacement, and refills when empty — so over each cycle every outcome appears exactly its intended number of times and long droughts are impossible; Tetris piece generation is the canonical case. A pity timer instead raises the probability of a rare outcome on each consecutive failure, so the drop rate is low early and approaches certainty at the cap, giving a bounded worst case; this is what most gacha and loot systems actually run, and the headline percentage they advertise is the average over that ramp rather than a per-roll constant. Neither is documented in a paper, and both matter more to perceived quality than almost any generator in the catalogue.
algorithms.citation: Game development practice. No canonical publication; described in GDC talks and design writing.

algorithms.name: √3 subdivision
algorithms.summary: Insert one vertex per triangle and flip every original edge. Triples the triangle count per round instead of quadrupling it.
algorithms.eli5: Splitting every triangle into four makes the mesh grow very fast — four times bigger each round. Instead, drop one new point in the middle of each triangle, join it to the three corners, and then flip each of the original edges so the triangles line up neatly. The mesh only grows three times per round, so you can stop closer to the size you actually wanted.
algorithms.description: One vertex per face, connected to that face's three corners, followed by an edge flip of every original edge; original vertices are then repositioned by a valence-dependent average. Triangle count multiplies by three rather than four, so two rounds of √3 give a finer granularity of control than one round of Loop and a coarser one than two — the practical motivation, since a 4× jump is often more refinement than wanted. Two rounds of √3 amount to a uniform 1-to-9 split, and the scheme is C² on regular meshes. It also adapts to local refinement more naturally than 1-to-4 schemes, because inserting a face point does not force neighbouring faces to split, which is what makes it attractive for adaptive detail on generated terrain and for meshes that must be refined only where the viewer is looking.
algorithms.citation: Kobbelt, √3-subdivision, SIGGRAPH 2000, 103–112

algorithms.name: Squarified treemaps
algorithms.authors: Mark Bruls, Kees Huizing, Jarke van Wijk
algorithms.summary: Subdivides a rectangle into weighted sub-rectangles that stay close to square, instead of thin slivers.
algorithms.eli5: You have a rectangle and a list of numbers, and each number must get an area that size. Laying them out in strips gives horrible long slivers, so instead keep adding items to the current strip only while doing so keeps the shapes closer to square — then start a fresh strip.
algorithms.description: The original slice-and-dice treemap alternates horizontal and vertical cuts, which preserves ordering but produces long thin slivers that are hard to compare or click. The squarified variant instead greedily adds items to a row while the worst aspect ratio in that row keeps improving, and starts a new row as soon as it would get worse — laying rows along the shorter side of the remaining space. The result approximates squares, at the cost of no longer preserving input order. In generation it is the standard trick for subdividing a footprint into rooms or a block into building lots with sensible proportions, because a room of area A that is 1×A is useless and a room that is √A×√A is a room.
algorithms.citation: Bruls, Huizing & van Wijk, Squarified Treemaps, Proc. Joint Eurographics / IEEE TCVG Symposium on Visualization, 33–42

algorithms.name: Cassowary
algorithms.authors: Greg Badros, Alan Borning, Peter Stuckey
algorithms.summary: Incremental linear constraint solver with hard and soft constraints. The engine under Auto Layout.
algorithms.eli5: Layout as a tug of war. State what must be true — this panel sits eight pixels right of that one — and what you would merely prefer, each preference with a strength. When the window resizes, the solver re-satisfies every must and abandons the weakest preferences first, without redoing the whole calculation.
algorithms.description: An incremental variant of the dual simplex method built for interactive use: constraints are added and removed one at a time and the solution is repaired rather than recomputed, so it keeps up with a window being dragged. Its second contribution is a constraint hierarchy — constraints carry strengths, from required down through strong, medium and weak, and the solver satisfies all required ones while minimising violation of the rest by preference order. That is what makes it usable for layout, where 'this panel must be inside the window' is non-negotiable but 'these two should be equal width' is a preference that yields when space runs short. It is the solver behind Apple's Auto Layout and a great many web and GUI layout engines, which makes it one of the most widely executed constraint solvers in existence.
algorithms.citation: Badros, Borning & Stuckey, The Cassowary linear arithmetic constraint solving algorithm, ACM TOCHI 8(4), 267–306

algorithms.name: CIEDE2000 colour difference
algorithms.authors: M. Ronnier Luo, Guihua Cui, Bryan Rigg; standardised by the CIE
algorithms.summary: The corrected formula for how different two colours look, with weightings that fix CIELAB's known non-uniformities.
algorithms.eli5: Measuring colour difference as plain distance in a perceptual space is close but not right — it overestimates in the blues, and treats a difference in colourfulness as more visible than it really is at high saturation. So take the plain distance and apply a set of correction factors, one for lightness, one for chroma, one for hue, plus a rotation term for the blue region.
algorithms.description: Computed in CIELAB but with substantial machinery on top: separate weighting functions S_L, S_C and S_H that scale the lightness, chroma and hue differences according to where in the space the pair sits, and an interaction term R_T that rotates the difference ellipse in the blue-violet region where CIELAB is worst. The result correlates far better with visual assessment than plain CIELAB distance and is the reference against which industrial colour tolerance is specified. For generation it matters wherever "different enough" has to be decided automatically: generating a categorical palette whose entries are mutually distinguishable, checking that a procedural recolour has not collapsed two states into the same appearance, or verifying a colour-blind-safe scheme. Its cost is that it is not a metric — it violates the triangle inequality — so it cannot be used as the distance inside a clustering algorithm without care.
algorithms.citation: Luo, Cui & Rigg, The development of the CIE 2000 colour-difference formula: CIEDE2000, Color Research & Application 26(5), 340–350; CIE Publication 142

algorithms.name: CMA-ES
algorithms.summary: Evolution strategy that learns the shape of the search landscape by adapting a full covariance matrix.
algorithms.eli5: Instead of a population, keep a cloud: a centre point, plus a description of which directions the cloud is stretched in. Sample from it, see which samples did well, shift the centre towards them and re-stretch the cloud along whichever directions have been paying off. It learns the shape of the landscape while descending it.
algorithms.description: Sample a population from a multivariate Gaussian, evaluate, and then update not just the mean but the *covariance matrix* of that Gaussian from the successful samples — so the distribution stretches along directions that have been paying off and shrinks across directions that have not. It also maintains an evolution path, a smoothed record of where the mean has been moving, which lets it distinguish a genuine trend from noise and adapt the overall step size accordingly. The effect is that it learns the local scaling and correlation structure of the problem, making it near-invariant to how the parameters happen to be scaled or rotated — the practical reason it works on badly conditioned problems where plain evolution strategies stall. It is the default choice for continuous, derivative-free optimisation up to a few hundred dimensions.
algorithms.citation: Hansen & Ostermeier, Completely Derandomized Self-Adaptation in Evolution Strategies, Evolutionary Computation 9(2), 159–195

algorithms.name: Image quilting
algorithms.summary: Copy overlapping patches instead of pixels, then cut each join along its path of least difference.
algorithms.eli5: Copying one pixel at a time is slow, so copy whole squares that overlap their neighbours. The overlap will not match exactly, so instead of blending it, find the wiggly path through the overlap where the two versions differ least, and cut along that. The seam hides in whatever detail was already there.
algorithms.description: Place patches in raster order, each overlapping its already-placed neighbours, choosing among sample patches whose overlap region best matches what is already there. Then, rather than feathering the overlap — which blurs — find the minimum-cost path through it using dynamic programming over the squared difference, and cut along that path. The two ideas are separable and both mattered: patches instead of pixels bought two orders of magnitude of speed, and the min-cut seam bought quality that blending cannot, because a seam that follows existing structure is invisible while a blurred one is not. Quilting is also the origin of texture *transfer* — constrain the patch choice by a target image's brightness as well as by the overlap, and the sample's material is painted onto the target's form. In generation it remains the practical way to make a photographed material tileable or to extend it to arbitrary size.
algorithms.citation: Efros & Freeman, Image quilting for texture synthesis and transfer, SIGGRAPH 2001, 341–346

algorithms.name: L-system road networks
algorithms.summary: L-systems grow street networks from population and terrain maps, then shape grammars build the lots and buildings. Became CityEngine.
algorithms.eli5: The turtle draws roads instead of branches. At each step it consults two maps — how many people live around here, and what shape is the ground — then decides whether to carry straight on, swing round to follow a ridge, or split in two. Big roads get drawn first; small streets fill in the blocks they leave behind.
algorithms.description: An L-system proposes road segments, but every proposal passes through two filters before it is accepted. Global goals shape the overall pattern — follow population density gradients, or impose a grid, radial or organic street style. Local constraints then adjust the individual segment: snap its endpoint to a nearby intersection if it is close enough, shorten it to stop at water, reject it if the slope is impossible. That propose-then-correct loop is what stops the network looking like a fractal and makes it look surveyed. Once the road graph closes, the enclosed blocks are recursively subdivided into lots with street frontage, and a shape grammar builds a mass on each lot.
algorithms.citation: Procedural Modeling of Cities, SIGGRAPH '01

algorithms.name: Simplex noise
algorithms.summary: Replaces the hypercube lattice with a simplex grid, cutting corner count from 2^n to n+1. Fewer artefacts, far better scaling into 3D and 4D.
algorithms.eli5: The same trick as Perlin noise, played on a grid of triangles instead of squares. A triangle has fewer corners to ask, so it is faster, and it loses the square grid's habit of showing faint streaks along the axes.
algorithms.description: The cost of classic Perlin noise doubles with every dimension, because a hypercube in n dimensions has 2^n corners that all need interpolating. Simplex noise skews the input coordinates onto a lattice of simplices — the simplest shape that tiles a space, a triangle in 2D and a tetrahedron in 3D — which has only n+1 corners. Contributions from each corner are summed with a radial falloff rather than interpolated along axes, so there is no axis-aligned interpolation to leave grid artefacts. Complexity drops from O(2^n) to O(n²), which is what makes 4D noise (3D plus time, for animated volumes) practical at all. Perlin patented it, which is why OpenSimplex exists as an unencumbered alternative.
algorithms.citation: Noise Hardware, in Real-Time Shading SIGGRAPH Course Notes, 2001

algorithms.name: Tessendorf ocean spectra
algorithms.summary: Synthesise ocean surface in the frequency domain from an empirical wave spectrum, then inverse FFT to a heightfield.
algorithms.eli5: The sea is not a set of waves you can draw. It is a recipe: for each wave size and direction, how much of it there is, measured from real oceans. Add thousands of those waves together in one enormous shortcut and out comes a patch of sea surface that looks right because it was measured, not invented.
algorithms.description: Rather than simulating water, synthesise a height field whose statistics match measured ocean. Start in the frequency domain: fill a complex grid with Gaussian random values scaled by the Phillips spectrum, an empirical model of how wave energy distributes across wavelength and direction given wind speed and fetch. Animate by rotating each frequency's phase according to the dispersion relation, which is what makes long waves travel faster than short ones — the detail that separates convincing ocean from moving noise. An inverse FFT returns the heightfield. Adding a horizontal displacement derived from the same spectrum produces Gerstner-like sharpened crests. It is the standard for both film and games, and it is a clear case of imitating measured statistics rather than deriving from physics.
algorithms.citation: Tessendorf, Simulating Ocean Water, SIGGRAPH course notes (1999–2004) — course notes, not a peer-reviewed paper

algorithms.name: Dual contouring
algorithms.authors: Tao Ju, Frank Losasso, Scott Schaefer, Joe Warren
algorithms.summary: Positions one vertex per cell by least-squares fitting the surface normals on its edges, so sharp edges and corners survive.
algorithms.eli5: Like the above, one point per cube — except you choose where that point goes by asking which way all the little surface fragments crossing this cube are facing, and solving for the spot that suits them all. If a genuine sharp edge runs through the cube, the solution lands exactly on it, so hard edges survive.
algorithms.description: Like surface nets it puts one vertex per cell, but it decides where by using Hermite data — not just where the surface crosses each edge, but the surface normal at that crossing. Each crossing defines a plane the surface should lie on; the vertex is placed at the point minimising squared distance to all of them, solved as a small least-squares system. Where the crossings agree the solution is a flat patch; where two or three planes meet at an angle the minimiser lands exactly on the crease or corner. That is the whole trick: normals carry the information that positions alone lose, so a cube comes out of the field as a cube rather than a rounded lump. The quadratic form can be degenerate on flat regions and needs regularising.
algorithms.citation: Dual contouring of Hermite data, ACM Transactions on Graphics 21(3) (SIGGRAPH 2002)

algorithms.name: Improved Perlin noise
algorithms.summary: Perlin noise with a better interpolant and a fixed set of gradients. Removes the visible grid artefacts of the 1985 version.
algorithms.eli5: The original recipe had two flaws that showed up as faint square patterns. Its fade curve had a kink in its rate of change, which the eye catches along grid lines, and its random directions clustered towards the corners of a cube. Swap in a smoother fade curve and a fixed set of evenly spread directions, and the grid disappears.
algorithms.description: Two changes to the 1985 construction, each fixing a visible artefact. The original used the cubic 3t²−2t³, whose second derivative is non-zero at the ends, so a normal map derived from the noise shows discontinuities on the lattice planes; the replacement quintic 6t⁵−15t⁴+10t³ has zero first *and* second derivative at 0 and 1, which removes them. And instead of normalising random vectors — which distributes directions unevenly, biased towards cube corners — gradients are chosen from the 12 midpoints of a cube's edges, which are evenly spread and let the dot products be computed by additions rather than multiplications. Perlin also replaced the permutation-table lookup with a bit-manipulation hash. This is the version in Perlin's reference Java implementation and therefore the one nearly every "Perlin noise" library actually implements, which makes the distinction easy to miss: the 1985 paper and the code everyone runs are not the same algorithm.
algorithms.citation: Perlin, Improving noise, ACM TOG 21(3) (SIGGRAPH 2002), 681–682

algorithms.name: Least-squares conformal maps
algorithms.authors: Bruno Lévy, Sylvain Petitjean, Nicolas Ray, Jérome Maillot
algorithms.summary: Flatten a surface into UV space by solving one sparse linear system that minimises angular distortion.
algorithms.eli5: You want to peel a 3D surface flat so you can paint on it, like flattening an orange skin. You cannot do it without stretching, so decide what to protect: keep every corner's *angles* as close to right as possible, and let the sizes stretch. That turns out to be one big set of simultaneous equations, and solving it once gives the whole flattening.
algorithms.description: Conformal maps preserve angles locally. Writing the discrete Cauchy–Riemann condition per triangle and minimising its squared violation over the whole chart gives a sparse least-squares problem, linear in the unknown UV coordinates, solvable in one shot once two vertices are pinned to remove the translation, rotation and scale freedom. There is no iteration and no per-triangle nonlinear solve, which is why it was the method that made automatic UV unwrapping practical. Angles are preserved but areas are not, so long thin charts can scale wildly along their length, and the pinned vertices influence the result — both addressed by later methods (ABF++, ARAP, and area-aware variants). For generated geometry this is the step that makes a procedural mesh texturable at all, and it is why the practical pipeline is: cut the surface into charts, flatten each with something like LSCM, then pack the charts into an atlas.
algorithms.citation: Lévy, Petitjean, Ray & Maillot, Least squares conformal maps for automatic texture atlas generation, ACM TOG 21(3) (SIGGRAPH 2002), 362–371

algorithms.name: Weighted Voronoi stippling
algorithms.summary: Lloyd relaxation weighted by image darkness, so stipple density follows tone.
algorithms.eli5: You want to redraw a photograph as thousands of ink dots, crowded in the shadows. Scatter dots, give each the region of the picture nearest to it, then move each dot to the *darkness-weighted* middle of its region. Repeat, and the dots migrate into the dark areas by themselves.
algorithms.description: Scatter points over the image, then run Lloyd relaxation — but instead of moving each point to the geometric centroid of its Voronoi cell, move it to the centroid weighted by image darkness, treating pixel intensity as a density function. Points therefore drift toward dark regions and spread apart in light ones. After a few iterations the stipple density reproduces the source tone while the spacing stays even and non-gridded, which is precisely what a human stippler achieves by eye. It is a neat demonstration that a single change of weighting turns a geometric relaxation into a tone-reproduction algorithm.
algorithms.citation: Weighted Voronoi Stippling, NPAR 2002, 37–43

algorithms.name: Fractal flames
algorithms.summary: IFS with non-linear variations, log-density tone mapping and structural colouring. The Apophysis look.
algorithms.eli5: The same dot-and-random-rule game, but bendy rules are allowed as well as shrinking ones, and instead of merely marking each spot you count how many times it was visited. Bright where the dots crowd, dim where they wander, which is why these look lit rather than drawn.
algorithms.description: Three changes to a plain iterated function system, each responsible for part of the aesthetic. First, the affine maps are composed with non-linear 'variations' — sinusoidal, spherical, swirl and dozens more — so the attractor curves and folds instead of staying piecewise-linear. Second, rather than plotting points as binary hits, accumulate a density histogram and tone-map it logarithmically, which preserves detail across the enormous dynamic range between the dense core and the faint outer wisps. Third, carry a colour coordinate along with each point, updated by whichever transform was applied, so hue encodes the history of the trajectory rather than its position. Together they turn a mathematical curiosity into the most recognisable style in generative art.
algorithms.citation: The Fractal Flame Algorithm, 2003 (revised 2008)

algorithms.name: Graph-cut textures
algorithms.authors: Vivek Kwatra, Arno Schödl, Irfan Essa, Greg Turk, Aaron Bobick
algorithms.summary: Choose the seam between two overlapping patches by solving a minimum graph cut — in 2D, and in 3D for video.
algorithms.eli5: Quilting cuts each seam along a path, which works when the patches are laid out in tidy rows. But if patches can overlap any which way, the boundary is a shape, not a path. So build a network where every pixel in the overlap chooses a side, and cutting the network in the cheapest possible place gives the best boundary — even one that loops back on itself.
algorithms.description: Where image quilting finds a minimum-cost path with dynamic programming, this formulates seam placement as a labelling problem: every pixel in the overlap is assigned to one patch or the other, with a cost for disagreeing with a neighbour proportional to how differently the two patches look there. Minimising that energy is exactly a minimum graph cut, solvable optimally in polynomial time, and unlike a path it can produce boundaries of any topology — islands, holes, patches inserted into the middle of other patches. That freedom lets patches be placed in arbitrary order and position rather than in raster scan, and it extends directly to three dimensions, which is what makes video texture synthesis possible with the same machinery. It is the seam-placement half of the problem stated in its general form, and its practical descendants are everywhere in panorama stitching, object removal and terrain patch blending.
algorithms.citation: Kwatra, Schödl, Essa, Turk & Bobick, Graphcut textures: image and video synthesis using graph cuts, ACM TOG 22(3) (SIGGRAPH 2003), 277–286

algorithms.name: Poisson image editing
algorithms.authors: Patrick Pérez, Michel Gangnet, Andrew Blake
algorithms.summary: Paste a region by matching its gradients, not its values, and solving for the values that fit. Seams disappear.
algorithms.eli5: Pasting a patch into a picture leaves a visible edge because the patch's brightness does not match its surroundings. So do not paste the brightnesses at all — paste only the *changes* from pixel to pixel, and then work backwards to find the brightnesses that both produce those changes and match the border exactly. The patch shifts its own tone to fit, and the seam vanishes.
algorithms.description: Take the gradient field of the source region as the target, fix the values on the boundary to those of the destination, and solve for the interior values whose gradient best matches — which is a Poisson equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions, one sparse linear solve per channel. Because only gradients are transferred, absolute intensity is free to shift, so the inserted region relights itself to its new surroundings and the seam disappears without any feathering. Variants fall out of manipulating the guidance field rather than the solver: mixing source and destination gradients pastes transparent or textured content, zeroing selected gradients removes objects, and amplifying them enhances local contrast. In procedural work this is the general answer to joining generated tiles or patches whose overall levels differ — the gradient-domain half of seam removal, complementary to the pixel-selection half that graph-cut textures solve.
algorithms.citation: Pérez, Gangnet & Blake, Poisson image editing, ACM TOG 22(3) (SIGGRAPH 2003), 313–318

algorithms.name: Potrace
algorithms.summary: Bitmap to vector: trace boundaries, fit an optimal polygon, then smooth into Bézier curves.
algorithms.eli5: Turning a pixel drawing into smooth curves, in three passes. First trace the staircase outline of the black pixels. Then work out the longest straight-ish runs that staircase could have stood for, and join them into a polygon. Finally round the polygon's corners into curves. Each pass throws away one kind of pixelness.
algorithms.description: Three stages. First decompose the bitmap into closed paths along the boundaries between black and white, using a consistent turn policy so ambiguous diagonal crossings resolve the same way everywhere. Second, approximate each path by an optimal polygon — optimal in the sense of minimising the number of segments subject to each segment staying within the pixel boundary, solved as a shortest-path problem rather than greedily, which is what stops the output looking stair-stepped. Third, classify each polygon vertex as a corner or a smooth point and fit Bézier segments accordingly, so curves come out curved and corners stay sharp. It is the standard raster-to-vector path, and the middle stage — global optimisation rather than local fitting — is the part that distinguishes it from naive tracers.
algorithms.citation: Selinger, Potrace: a polygon-based tracing algorithm, 2003

algorithms.name: Xorshift
algorithms.summary: Three shifts and three XORs. Among the fastest usable generators, and small enough to inline.
algorithms.eli5: The entire generator is three lines: shift the number, exclusive-or it with itself, three times over with different shift amounts. That is all of it. Wildly fast, small enough to memorise, and only just good enough — it fails some of the harder statistical tests, which is why its descendants add a final scramble.
algorithms.description: The state is a single machine word. Each step XORs the state with a shifted copy of itself, three times, with a carefully chosen triple of shift amounts — the choice determines whether the generator achieves its full period of 2^k−1. That is the entire algorithm: no multiplication, no memory beyond one register, and it compiles to a handful of instructions. Plain xorshift fails some statistical tests because the output is a linear function of the state over GF(2), which later scrambled variants (xorshift*, xoshiro) fix by applying a non-linear output transform. For procedural generation the appeal is that it is cheap enough to run per-pixel or per-voxel without thinking about cost.
algorithms.citation: Xorshift RNGs, Journal of Statistical Software 8(14), 1–6

algorithms.name: Level-set topology optimisation
algorithms.authors: Grégoire Allaire, François Jouve, Anca-Maria Toader
algorithms.summary: Represent the design as the zero level of a field and move that boundary along its shape derivative. Crisp edges throughout.
algorithms.eli5: Density methods leave a grey fuzz that has to be cleaned up at the end. Instead, describe the shape by a field where negative means solid and positive means empty — the shape is wherever the field is exactly zero. Work out which way to push the boundary to improve things, and push the field accordingly. The edge is always a real edge.
algorithms.description: The structure is the negative region of a level-set function on a fixed grid. Shape sensitivity analysis gives a velocity field on the boundary — the direction and rate at which moving each point of the surface would improve the objective — and advecting the level set by that velocity with a Hamilton–Jacobi update evolves the design. Because the boundary is implicit, topology changes such as holes merging or vanishing happen automatically, which is what shape-optimisation methods on explicit meshes cannot do. The trade against SIMP is real in both directions: the boundary stays sharp and physical quantities on it are meaningful, but new holes cannot nucleate from nowhere without extra machinery such as a topological derivative, so the initial guess matters much more. It is the natural formulation where the objective lives on the surface — heat transfer coefficients, fluid drag, optical scattering — and it is the same representation as the SDF concept, applied to optimisation rather than modelling.
algorithms.citation: Allaire, Jouve & Toader, Structural optimization using sensitivity analysis and a level-set method, Journal of Computational Physics 194(1), 363–393

algorithms.name: Droplet erosion
algorithms.authors: No single origin; many independent variants
algorithms.summary: Drop individual particles on the heightfield and let each carve its own path downhill.
algorithms.eli5: Instead of flooding the whole map at once, drop one raindrop somewhere and follow it. It rolls downhill, scooping up dirt as it speeds up and dropping it as it slows, until it dries up. Do that a million times with a million drops and valleys and rivers carve themselves.
algorithms.description: Instead of solving flow over the whole grid, spawn a droplet at a random point and follow it. It accelerates down the local gradient, picks up sediment in proportion to its speed and the steepness, deposits when it slows or when carrying more than its capacity, loses a little water to evaporation each step, and dies after a fixed lifetime. Run a few hundred thousand droplets and drainage networks emerge. It is far simpler to implement than grid-based hydraulic erosion and needs no global solve, which is why it dominates hobbyist and indie terrain code; the trade-off is that results depend on droplet count and seeding, and it is harder to reason about convergence. There is no origin paper — it is a simplification of the Musgrave and Mei models that spread through tutorials and blog posts.
algorithms.citation: No canonical publication. A particle simplification of grid hydraulic erosion; widely reimplemented from tutorials.

algorithms.name: Euclidean rhythms (Bjorklund)
algorithms.authors: Godfried Toussaint; algorithm by Eric Bjorklund
algorithms.summary: Distribute k onsets as evenly as possible over n beats using the Euclidean algorithm. Reproduces a great many traditional rhythms.
algorithms.eli5: Spread five beats as evenly as you can across sixteen slots. It does not divide, so use the ancient trick for finding a greatest common divisor and it spreads the awkwardness out evenly instead of dumping it at the end. Out come the rhythms of a startling number of traditional drum patterns.
algorithms.description: Given n beats and k onsets, the problem is to space the onsets as evenly as possible when k does not divide n. Bjorklund's algorithm — originally written for timing pulses in a neutron spallation source — solves it by the same repeated-remainder structure as Euclid's GCD: pair off groups of the two sequence types, recursing on the remainder, until at most one group is left over. Toussaint's contribution was the observation that the resulting patterns coincide with a striking number of traditional rhythms across West African, Latin American, Balkan and Middle Eastern music. E(3,8) is the tresillo, E(5,8) the cinquillo, E(5,16) the Brazilian bossa-nova pattern. Worth noting the catalogue overclaims this as producing 'most world rhythms'; Toussaint's claim is that many traditional rhythms are Euclidean, not most.
algorithms.citation: Toussaint, The Euclidean Algorithm Generates Traditional Musical Rhythms, Proc. BRIDGES 2005, 47–56

algorithms.name: Falling-sand automata
algorithms.authors: No single origin; formalised in Noita's Falling Everything engine
algorithms.summary: Per-pixel material simulation by local swap rules. Sand falls, water spreads, fire consumes fuel.
algorithms.eli5: Every grain of sand looks at the square below it. Empty? Fall. Blocked? Try down-left, then down-right. That is sand. Now say water also spreads sideways, fire turns neighbouring wood into fire, and water on fire makes steam — and you have a whole physics out of a handful of if-statements.
algorithms.description: Every pixel holds a material, and each is updated by rules that only inspect its immediate neighbours: sand moves down, or diagonally down if blocked; water does the same but also spreads sideways; gas rises; fire converts flammable neighbours and burns out. Ordering matters more than the rules do — updating a grid top-to-bottom makes falling material teleport in a single frame, so implementations scan bottom-up for falling materials, alternate scan direction per frame to remove left-right bias, and mark cells dirty to skip settled regions. It is not a cellular automaton in the strict sense, because updates are sequential and in-place rather than simultaneous, which is exactly what allows conservation of material. Noita's engine is the most complete realisation and the reason the technique is taken seriously as a game mechanic rather than a toy.
algorithms.citation: No origin paper. Nolla Games' Falling Everything engine is the reference implementation; described in their GDC talk.

algorithms.name: Reiter snowflake model
algorithms.summary: A two-parameter cellular automaton on a hexagonal grid producing genuinely six-fold dendritic snow crystals.
algorithms.eli5: Fill a honeycomb of hexagons with water vapour and freeze the middle one. Then repeat one rule: a hexagon freezes when enough of its neighbours already have, and freezing sucks the vapour out of the area around it. Arms grow, starve their own flanks, and split — which is why real snowflakes have six arms and no two match.
algorithms.description: Cells sit on a hexagonal lattice and hold a real value representing water. Cells adjacent to the frozen crystal are 'receptive'; their water is held and not diffused, and a constant addition term feeds them. All non-receptive cells diffuse toward the average of their neighbours. Each step, receptive cells that exceed one become part of the crystal. Just two parameters — the background vapour level and the addition constant — select the entire morphology, sweeping through plates, dendrites, stellar and sectored forms in a way that matches the real Nakaya diagram surprisingly well. It is a good example of a model that is genuinely mechanistic rather than imitative: the six-fold symmetry emerges from the lattice and the diffusion, and is not imposed.
algorithms.citation: A local cellular model for snow crystal growth, Chaos, Solitons & Fractals 23, 1111–1119

algorithms.name: Texture optimization
algorithms.authors: Vivek Kwatra, Irfan Essa, Aaron Bobick, Nipun Kwatra
algorithms.summary: Define a global energy — every output neighbourhood should resemble some sample neighbourhood — and minimise it everywhere at once.
algorithms.eli5: Every previous method builds the texture in some order and can never revisit an early decision. This one writes down a single score for the whole picture — how well does every little window in it match *some* window of the sample — and then improves the whole picture at once, over and over, until the score stops falling.
algorithms.description: The energy sums, over every overlapping neighbourhood of the output, the squared distance to that neighbourhood's nearest match in the sample. Minimisation alternates two steps: find each neighbourhood's nearest sample match, then set every output pixel to the weighted average of what all the overlapping matched neighbourhoods say it should be. That is an expectation-maximisation loop, run coarse-to-fine over an image pyramid, and it converges to a texture that is locally sample-like everywhere rather than only along the path the synthesis happened to take. The global formulation is what makes it controllable — add a term for matching a flow field and the texture aligns to it, add one for a target image and you get transfer, add one for the previous frame and you get temporally coherent video. It is slower than quilting and is the method most later work builds on, including the neural variants, which replace the pixel-neighbourhood distance with a learned feature distance and keep the loop.
algorithms.citation: Kwatra, Essa, Bobick & Kwatra, Texture optimization for example-based synthesis, ACM TOG 24(3) (SIGGRAPH 2005), 795–802

algorithms.name: Wavelet noise
algorithms.summary: Near-perfectly band-limited noise, fixing the aliasing and detail loss Perlin noise suffers under minification.
algorithms.eli5: Ordinary noise grows extra sparkle when you shrink it and goes mushy when you enlarge it. This version is built by blurring a random picture, subtracting the blur from the original and keeping only the difference, so every size of detail lives in its own drawer and cannot leak into another.
algorithms.description: Perlin noise is not actually band-limited — each octave leaks energy into frequencies above and below its nominal band. Minify it and the high leakage aliases into visible crawling; blur it and the low leakage means detail vanishes before it should. Wavelet noise fixes this by construction: generate a tile of random values, downsample it by half, upsample that back to full size, and subtract the result from the original. What remains is precisely the content that could not survive a halving — a single, clean octave band. Summing such bands with correct scaling gives noise where each octave can be faded in and out independently as the surface changes size on screen, which is what makes it hold up under both minification and projection of 3D noise onto a 2D surface.
algorithms.citation: Wavelet noise, ACM Transactions on Graphics 24(3), 803–811 (SIGGRAPH 2005)

algorithms.name: CGA shape grammars
algorithms.authors: Pascal Müller, Peter Wonka, Simon Haegler, Andreas Ulmer, Luc Van Gool
algorithms.summary: A split grammar for buildings: mass to floors to facade tiles to windows, with context-sensitive rules.
algorithms.eli5: A building starts as a plain box. One rule slices it into floors, the next slices each floor into bays, the next says a bay is a wall with a hole in it, and the last drops in a window. Because every rule works on whatever the previous rule made, a whole city comes out of a page of rules.
algorithms.description: Rules operate on labelled scopes — an oriented box with a coordinate frame. A rule either subdivides a scope along an axis into labelled child scopes, repeats a component across it, or replaces it with geometry. So a building mass splits into floors, a floor's front face splits into a row of facade tiles, a tile splits into window, sill and wall, and a window is finally instantiated as an asset. Context sensitivity is what lifted it above earlier split grammars: rules can query occlusion and neighbouring scopes, so a facade knows not to place a window where another building abuts it, and ground floors can differ from upper ones. Müller's team rebuilt Pompeii with it, and it became CityEngine. This is the archetype for the whole `architecture` domain of the catalogue.
algorithms.citation: Müller et al., Procedural modeling of buildings, ACM TOG 25(3) (SIGGRAPH '06), 614–623

algorithms.name: Jump flooding
algorithms.summary: Propagate nearest-seed information across a grid in log n passes with halving step sizes. Voronoi and distance fields on the GPU.
algorithms.eli5: Every square needs to know which seed is nearest. Ask the squares that are 64 steps away, then 32, then 16, then 8, and so on down to 1 — each time keeping the best seed you have heard about. After a handful of rounds everyone knows, and every square did its asking at the same moment as every other.
algorithms.description: Seed cells with their own coordinates and leave the rest empty. Then for step sizes n/2, n/4, … 1, each cell looks at its eight neighbours at that offset and keeps whichever candidate seed is closest to itself. Information travels a long way in the first passes and is refined in the last, so the whole field converges in log n rounds rather than the n rounds flood-filling would take. Every cell is independent within a pass, which is the point: this is how you compute a Voronoi diagram or a distance field on a GPU, where a sequential sweep would be worthless. It is approximate — a small number of cells can end up with the wrong nearest seed — and the paper quantifies the error, which is low enough that jump flooding is the standard technique for real-time SDF generation, soft shadows from silhouettes, and outline effects.
algorithms.citation: Rong & Tan, Jump flooding in GPU with applications to Voronoi diagram and distance transform, I3D 2006, 109–116

algorithms.name: Monte Carlo tree search
algorithms.authors: Rémi Coulom; UCT selection rule by Levente Kocsis and Csaba Szepesvári
algorithms.summary: Grow a search tree towards whatever is promising, judging each option by random play-outs rather than by a scoring function.
algorithms.eli5: You have a decision tree too big to explore. So play it out at random to the end, note who won, and record that along the path you took. Do it thousands of times, but bias where you start exploring towards the moves that have been doing well — while still occasionally trying neglected ones. The tree grows deepest where it matters.
algorithms.description: Four steps per iteration: descend the existing tree choosing children by a rule balancing observed value against how rarely they have been tried, expand one new node, run a random play-out from it to a terminal state, and back up the result along the visited path. The UCT selection rule makes the balance principled by treating each node as a multi-armed bandit. The property that matters is that no evaluation function is required — the only domain knowledge needed is the rules and a terminal outcome — and the search is anytime, improving monotonically with more iterations and interruptible at any point. For generation it belongs here rather than under game AI because it is a search over constructions: it has been used to build levels tile by tile, to generate puzzles by searching for instances a solver finds hard, to lay out dungeons under reachability constraints, and to assemble decks and rulesets, all cases where the objective is only computable by finishing the artefact and testing it. The tension worth naming is that this concept is called search-based PCG but described as generate-evaluate-mutate; MCTS is search without a population, and it fits the name rather than the description.
algorithms.citation: Coulom, Efficient selectivity and backup operators in Monte-Carlo tree search, Computers and Games 2006, 72–83; UCT from Kocsis & Szepesvári, Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning, ECML 2006

algorithms.name: Poisson surface reconstruction
algorithms.authors: Michael Kazhdan, Matthew Bolitho, Hugues Hoppe
algorithms.summary: Treat oriented points as samples of a surface gradient and solve for the field whose gradient best matches them.
algorithms.eli5: You have a cloud of measured points, each with a little arrow saying which way is 'out'. Rather than joining the points up, look for the smooth in-or-out field across all of space whose own arrows best agree with the measured ones. Solve that once, then take the surface where the field crosses the middle. Noise and holes get smoothed over for free, because you asked for the best global fit rather than a local join.
algorithms.description: The indicator function of a solid — one inside, zero outside — has a gradient that is zero everywhere except at the surface, where it is the inward normal. Reverse that: given oriented sample points, build a vector field approximating that gradient, then find the scalar field whose gradient best matches it in the least-squares sense. Taking the divergence turns this into a Poisson equation, discretised on an adaptive octree with a hierarchy of smooth basis functions and solved with a multigrid method, after which the surface comes out by isosurfacing. Because the formulation is global, noise averages out and holes are filled by the smoothest plausible continuation rather than by a local heuristic — the property that made it the default in photogrammetry and LiDAR pipelines and put it inside MeshLab, CloudCompare and Open3D. The trade is that it never reproduces a sharp crease exactly, and it will confidently close a hole that should have stayed open.
algorithms.citation: Kazhdan, Bolitho & Hoppe, Poisson surface reconstruction, Eurographics Symposium on Geometry Processing 2006, 61–70

algorithms.name: Bridson Poisson disk sampling
algorithms.summary: Blue-noise point sets in O(N) and in any dimension, by throwing darts only near existing samples.
algorithms.eli5: Scatter dots so that no two are ever closer than some distance. Keep a list of dots that might still have room around them. Take one off the list, fire a few dozen tries into a ring around it, keep the first try that clears everything — and if none of them works, cross that dot off for good.
algorithms.description: Naive dart throwing — propose a random point, reject it if it is too close to any existing one — gets exponentially slower as the space fills. Bridson's change is to only ever propose points near an existing sample. Keep an active list. Repeatedly pick a random active sample and try k candidates (k=30 works) uniformly in the annulus between r and 2r around it; accept the first that is at least r from every existing sample, and add it to the active list. If all k fail, that sample is surrounded, so remove it from the active list. A background grid with cells of side r/√n holds at most one sample each, so the neighbour check is a constant number of cell lookups. The result is O(N), works in any dimension, and produces the even-but-not-gridded spacing that scattering vegetation, stars and stipples actually wants.
algorithms.citation: Fast Poisson disk sampling in arbitrary dimensions, ACM SIGGRAPH 2007 sketches

algorithms.name: Curl noise
algorithms.authors: Robert Bridson, Jim Houriham, Marcus Nordenstam
algorithms.summary: Take the curl of a noise potential field. The result is exactly incompressible — turbulent flow without simulating fluid.
algorithms.eli5: You want to swirl dust around without it ever piling up or thinning out. Build a bumpy hill out of noise, then at every point travel *along* the hill's contour lines instead of up or down them. Nothing can accumulate, because you only ever move sideways — and it looks exactly like smoke.
algorithms.description: Build a vector potential out of noise, then take its curl to get the velocity field. The curl of any field is divergence-free as a mathematical identity, so the resulting flow has no sources or sinks anywhere — particles advected through it swirl and never bunch up or thin out, which is exactly what incompressible fluid looks like. No solver, no pressure projection, no timestep: the field is a closed-form function of position and can be sampled independently at any point, which makes it trivially parallel and stable. Boundaries are handled by ramping the potential to zero near an obstacle, which makes flow slide along its surface instead of through it. It is the standard cheat for smoke, dust and magic.
algorithms.citation: Curl-Noise for Procedural Fluid Flow, ACM TOG 26(3) (SIGGRAPH 2007)

algorithms.name: Mei GPU hydraulic erosion
algorithms.authors: Xing Mei, Philippe Decaudin, Bao-Gang Hu
algorithms.summary: Shallow-water flow on the GPU driving erosion and deposition, fast enough to watch happen.
algorithms.eli5: The same erosion, rewritten so that every cell can be updated in the same instant as every other — because that is precisely what a graphics card is good at. Water depth, flow speed, carried sediment and ground height are four pictures, and each step is a handful of simple picture-to-picture operations.
algorithms.description: Rather than moving sediment by comparing neighbouring heights, this solves a shallow-water model to get an actual velocity field. Each cell holds terrain height, water height, sediment and outflow flux in four directions; a step computes flux from height differences, updates water depth, derives velocity, then uses that velocity to decide erosion or deposition via a sediment capacity term, and finally advects the suspended sediment along the flow. Every stage is a local grid operation, so the whole thing maps onto fragment shaders and runs interactively. Having a real velocity field rather than a slope heuristic is what produces meandering channels and proper deposition fans, and interactivity changes erosion from an overnight bake into something you can art-direct.
algorithms.citation: Fast Hydraulic Erosion Simulation and Visualization on GPU, Pacific Graphics 2007

algorithms.name: Model synthesis
algorithms.summary: Generate large models consistent with the local adjacency structure of a small example. Predates and closely resembles Wave Function Collapse.
algorithms.eli5: You have one example building made of blocks. Write down, for every pair of blocks that touch in it, that those two are allowed to touch. Now fill a fresh empty space with blocks obeying nothing but that list. What comes out is new, and yet every single join in it was copied from something that already worked.
algorithms.description: Read an example model and record, for every pair of adjacent tiles, that the pairing is legal — the example is treated as a specification of what may touch what, not as something to copy. Then assign tiles to the output so that every adjacency in it appears somewhere in the example. Solving the whole output at once is intractable, so it proceeds in overlapping subregions, freezing each once it is consistent and using it as boundary conditions for the next. That windowing is what keeps large outputs feasible, and it is the main structural difference from the later WFC, which collapses one cell at a time across the whole grid.
algorithms.citation: Merrell, model synthesis (PhD work); see overview

algorithms.name: Position-based dynamics
algorithms.authors: Matthias Müller, Bruno Heidelberger, Marcus Hennix, John Ratcliff
algorithms.summary: Skip forces entirely — project positions to satisfy constraints directly. Unconditionally stable, trivially controllable.
algorithms.eli5: Forget forces. Move everything wherever it wants to go, then repeatedly fix up whatever that broke — these two cloth points have drifted too far apart, so pull them back a bit. A few rounds of fixing gives cloth and rope that can never explode, because every move you make is towards being correct.
algorithms.description: Force-based integration overshoots when constraints are stiff, which is why cloth explodes at large timesteps. PBD removes the force layer: predict positions from current velocity, then iteratively project those positions to satisfy each constraint directly — for a distance constraint, simply move the two particles along their connecting line until they are the right distance apart, weighted by inverse mass. Derive velocities afterwards from how far positions actually moved. Because nothing integrates a force, nothing can overshoot, and stiffness becomes just the number of solver iterations. Collisions are handled by the same mechanism, projecting penetrating points out. This trade of physical accuracy for stability and control is why PBD and its extension XPBD dominate real-time cloth, rope, soft bodies and hair in games.
algorithms.citation: Müller, Heidelberger, Hennix & Ratcliff, Position based dynamics, J. Visual Communication and Image Representation 18(2), 109–118

algorithms.name: Space colonisation
algorithms.authors: Adam Runions, Brendan Lane, Przemyslaw Prusinkiewicz
algorithms.summary: Buds compete to fill empty volume. Breaks the symmetry inherent in L-systems and gives far more realistic crowns.
algorithms.eli5: Fill the space where you want a tree to be with a cloud of invisible target points. Every branch tip looks at the targets nearest to it and grows towards their average; reached targets are deleted. Branches avoid each other naturally, because they are eating each other's targets, and the crown fills the shape you drew.
algorithms.description: Scatter attraction points through the volume the tree should fill. Each iteration, every attraction point looks for the nearest branch tip within its influence radius and votes for it; every tip that received votes grows one segment in the average direction of its voters. Any attraction point that comes within a kill distance of a tip is removed, since that space is now occupied. The competition is the whole mechanism — two tips reaching for the same region starve each other, so branches naturally space themselves, avoid collisions, and fill the crown evenly without any explicit rule saying they should. Change the shape of the attractor cloud and you change the species. It extends the authors' earlier leaf venation model into three dimensions.
algorithms.citation: Modeling Trees with a Space Colonization Algorithm, Eurographics Workshop on Natural Phenomena 2007

algorithms.name: Domain warping
algorithms.authors: Íñigo Quílez (widely used earlier; this is the canonical write-up)
algorithms.summary: Feed noise into the coordinates of other noise. One line of code, and the source of marble, magma and silk.
algorithms.eli5: Rather than changing the picture, change where you look at it. Ask the noise for its value not at the point you wanted but at a point shoved sideways by some *other* noise. Straight things start to swirl and drift, which is what makes marble, smoke and wood grain look pulled around rather than sprinkled on.
algorithms.description: Instead of evaluating noise at a point, evaluate it at a point that has itself been displaced by another noise field: f(p + g(p)). Nest it and you get f(p + g(p + h(p))). Each level of nesting stretches and folds the domain, turning the isotropic blobbiness of plain fBm into flowing, filamentary structure — which is why marble veins, magma, smoke and silk all come from the same two-line change. The reason it works is that warping preserves the statistics of the source field while destroying its isotropy, so the result still reads as natural but has direction and flow that noise alone never produces. There is no origin paper; it is folklore formalised by Quílez's article, which is exactly the kind of technique the paper-only rule was excluding.
algorithms.citation: Quílez, "Domain warping", iquilezles.org — an article, not a peer-reviewed paper

algorithms.name: SDF primitive and operator library
algorithms.authors: Íñigo Quílez and the Shadertoy community
algorithms.summary: Closed-form distance functions for primitives, plus min/max operators for combining them. The vocabulary of raymarched scenes.
algorithms.eli5: A library of one-line answers to "how far am I from this shape?". A sphere is your distance from its centre minus its radius, and so on. Then a few ways to combine answers: the smaller of two is a union, the larger is an intersection, and blending them smoothly is a weld. Whole scenes get built with no geometry at all.
algorithms.description: A signed distance function returns, for any point, the distance to the nearest surface — negative inside. Primitives have exact closed forms: a sphere is length(p) − r, a box is a few max operations on the absolute components. Combination is then set algebra on distances: union is min, intersection is max, subtraction is max(a, −b). Rounding any shape is subtracting a constant; shelling is taking the absolute value and subtracting; infinite repetition is applying modulo to the input coordinate before evaluating, which tiles a scene at no cost. That last property is why raymarched scenes can contain unbounded detail in a few kilobytes. The collected library is a reference implementation rather than a paper — Quílez's articles and the Shadertoy corpus are the canonical source — but it is the substrate of an entire practice.
algorithms.citation: Quílez, distance function articles at iquilezles.org, plus the Shadertoy corpus. Reference implementation, not a paper.

algorithms.name: Wavelet turbulence
algorithms.authors: Theodore Kim, Nils Thürey, Doug James, Markus Gross
algorithms.summary: Simulate coarsely, then synthesise the missing fine detail by extrapolating the energy spectrum. Detail without the simulation cost.
algorithms.eli5: A cheap smoke simulation has the big swirls right but is missing all the fine curls, because the grid is too coarse to hold them. Rather than simulating on a huge grid, look at how much energy the small swirls you *can* see have, use the known physical rule for how that falls off, and add in invented curls at the right strength. The added detail moves with the flow, so it looks simulated.
algorithms.description: Decompose the coarse simulated velocity field with a wavelet transform to measure how energy is distributed across the scales that were resolved. Kolmogorov's theory says turbulent kinetic energy falls off as k^(−5/3), so the energy at the unresolved scales can be extrapolated rather than computed. Synthesise those scales as divergence-free curl noise, scaled to the extrapolated energy and weighted to appear only where the simulation was actually turbulent, then advect the synthetic detail along with the flow using a texture-coordinate field that is periodically regenerated to avoid unbounded stretching. The result is high-frequency detail that is spatially and temporally coherent with the underlying simulation at a fraction of the cost of simulating at that resolution, and it made the "simulate low, upres high" pipeline standard in film smoke and fire. It also depends directly on curl noise, already in this table, which is what supplies the incompressible synthetic band.
algorithms.citation: Kim, Thürey, James & Gross, Wavelet turbulence for fluid simulation, ACM TOG 27(3) (SIGGRAPH 2008)

algorithms.name: WCAG relative luminance contrast
algorithms.summary: A contrast ratio from relative luminance, with fixed thresholds. The check any generated palette has to pass.
algorithms.eli5: Text has to be readable against its background. So work out how much light each of the two colours sends out, add a small amount to both to account for screen glare, and divide the brighter by the darker. The answer runs from 1 (identical) to 21 (black on white), and there are fixed numbers you must beat.
algorithms.description: Linearise each sRGB channel, weight them 0.2126/0.7152/0.0722 to get relative luminance, then form (L_lighter + 0.05) / (L_darker + 0.05). The 0.05 offsets model ambient screen flare and are what stop the ratio running to infinity against pure black. Thresholds are 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text at level AA. This is the single most consequential colour computation in generated interfaces, because it is the one that is legally cited, and any theme, token scale or dark-mode derivation that does not enforce it produces output that cannot ship. It is also known to be wrong in specific ways — it is a luminance ratio rather than a perceptual model, so it over-rates dark-on-light pairs and under-rates light-on-dark, which is why the APCA candidate algorithm exists and why generators that only satisfy WCAG can still produce combinations that read badly.
algorithms.citation: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.0 (2008), success criterion 1.4.3 and the relative luminance definition; carried unchanged into WCAG 2.1 and 2.2

algorithms.name: Gabor noise
algorithms.authors: Ares Lagae, Sylvain Lefebvre, George Drettakis, Philip Dutré
algorithms.summary: Sparse convolution with a Gabor kernel, giving direct control of orientation, frequency and bandwidth.
algorithms.eli5: Instead of random numbers on a grid, sprinkle thousands of tiny ripples — each a little wave with its own direction and size — and add them all up. Because you chose the wave sizes yourself, you know exactly how fine or coarse the result is, which none of the other recipes can promise.
algorithms.description: Instead of interpolating a lattice, scatter randomly positioned kernels through space and sum them — sparse convolution noise. The kernel here is a Gabor kernel: a sinusoid multiplied by a Gaussian envelope. Because the Fourier transform of that kernel is a Gaussian centred on the sinusoid's frequency, the noise's power spectrum is known in closed form and is set directly by the kernel's parameters. That means orientation, principal frequency and bandwidth become explicit dials rather than emergent side effects, so you can ask for anisotropic streaks at a specific angle, or a narrow band with no harmonics. Lattice noises give you whatever spectrum their construction happens to produce; this gives you the one you asked for. The cost is that it is considerably slower.
algorithms.citation: Procedural Noise using Sparse Gabor Convolution, ACM TOG 28(3), 54–64 (SIGGRAPH 2009)

algorithms.name: PatchMatch
algorithms.authors: Connelly Barnes, Eli Shechtman, Adam Finkelstein, Dan Goldman
algorithms.summary: Find approximate nearest-neighbour patches for a whole image by guessing once, then propagating good guesses to neighbours.
algorithms.eli5: Every method above needs to know, for each little window, which window of the sample matches it best — and searching for that is the slow part. The trick: guess randomly for every window at once. Then have each window ask its neighbour "where did you find your match?", because if your neighbour found a good one, the spot just next to it is probably good for you. A few rounds of asking, plus a few random tries, and almost everything has found its match.
algorithms.description: Three ideas. Initialise every patch's correspondence at random. Then propagate: scan the image and let each patch test the offsets its already-scanned neighbours are using, since natural images are piecewise smooth and a good offset for one patch is usually good for the patch beside it. Then random search: test a few candidates at exponentially decreasing distances around the current best, which escapes local minima. Alternating scan directions and repeating a handful of times converges to an approximate nearest-neighbour field orders of magnitude faster than tree-based search, in memory proportional to the image. Because it makes correspondence cheap, it made interactive versions of everything above possible — this is the algorithm inside content-aware fill, reshuffling, retargeting, and most modern inpainting that is not a neural network. Its generalisation to arbitrary descriptors and to 3D makes it a general correspondence tool rather than only a texture one.
algorithms.citation: Barnes, Shechtman, Finkelstein & Goldman, PatchMatch: a randomized correspondence algorithm for structural image editing, ACM TOG 28(3) (SIGGRAPH 2009)

algorithms.name: Recast navmesh generation
algorithms.summary: Voxelise level geometry, filter by walkability, then region-grow and triangulate into a navigation mesh.
algorithms.eli5: Given a world made of arbitrary geometry, work out where a character can actually walk. Turn everything into a stack of solid slabs, discard any surface too steep or with too little headroom above it, shrink what is left inwards by the character's own width, and convert the remainder into walkable polygons.
algorithms.description: Rasterise all collision geometry into a heightfield of voxel spans. Mark spans walkable by slope and by whether there is enough clearance above them, then erode the walkable surface inward by the agent radius so the agent can be treated as a point thereafter. Partition the remaining surface into regions — by watershed, monotone or layer partitioning — trace the contours of each region, simplify them, and triangulate into a convex-polygon mesh that Detour can path over. The pipeline matters because it is fully automatic: it takes arbitrary geometry, including geometry a procedural generator just produced, and yields navigable space with no hand annotation. It ships in Unity, Unreal and Godot, which makes it one of the most widely deployed pieces of generation infrastructure in games.
algorithms.citation: Mononen, Recast & Detour navigation toolset, open source, 2009

algorithms.name: Alea
algorithms.summary: A multiply-with-carry generator designed for JavaScript, avoiding the language's lack of 64-bit integers.
algorithms.eli5: A generator written for JavaScript back when JavaScript had no whole numbers at all, only decimals. It keeps three fractional numbers and shuffles their digits about by multiplying, which sidesteps the missing arithmetic entirely. Fast, seedable from a word, and everywhere in browser generative art.
algorithms.description: JavaScript has no integer type — all numbers are doubles — so the bit-twiddling that PRNGs elsewhere rely on either breaks or runs slowly. Alea sidesteps this by using multiply-with-carry arithmetic that stays inside the 53 bits a double represents exactly, producing well-distributed floats directly rather than integers that must then be converted. It seeds from arbitrary strings via a small hash, which is what made it the default choice for seeded generation in browsers before better options existed. Baagøe's original page is gone, so the reference is now the surviving implementations; it is included here because it is genuinely distinct from the xorshift and PCG families rather than a port of them, and because it is what a large amount of existing JavaScript procedural code actually uses.
algorithms.citation: Baagøe, Alea PRNG, c. 2010. Original page defunct; survives as reference implementations.

algorithms.name: MaxRects bin packing
algorithms.summary: Track the set of maximal free rectangles, place each item into the best one, then split what remains.
algorithms.eli5: Packing rectangles onto a sheet. Keep a list of every empty rectangle still available. To place a piece, choose the free rectangle it fits most snugly into, put it there, and then split every free rectangle it overlapped into the smaller pieces that are still empty.
algorithms.description: Maintain a list of maximal free rectangles — every free area that cannot be extended in any direction. To place an item, score every free rectangle it fits in by some heuristic (smallest leftover short side, smallest area, lowest top edge) and take the best. Then split: every free rectangle overlapping the placement is cut into the pieces that remain, and any resulting rectangle contained inside another is pruned. Keeping the maximal set rather than a disjoint partition is what gives it the edge over shelf and guillotine methods, because it never loses a placement opportunity that spans what would otherwise be two separate free regions. This is what sprite atlas packers and texture-atlas tooling actually run. Published as a survey and reference implementation rather than a peer-reviewed paper.
algorithms.citation: Jylänki, A Thousand Ways to Pack the Bin — A Practical Approach to Two-Dimensional Rectangle Bin Packing, 2010

algorithms.name: Physarum transport networks
algorithms.summary: Particles deposit and follow a decaying trail. Produces the minimal transport networks slime mould is famous for.
algorithms.eli5: Thousands of imaginary specks, each leaving a faint trail behind it and each steering towards the strongest trail it can smell ahead. Trails fade with time. Well-used routes get reinforced and everything else disappears, so the specks collectively find a tidy network between food sources without any one of them knowing the map.
algorithms.description: Each particle has a position and heading, and does two things: it deposits a chemoattractant trail at its location, and it samples the trail field at three sensors ahead of it, turning toward whichever reads strongest. The field diffuses and decays. That is the whole model — no graph, no global optimisation, no notion of a network — and yet the population self-organises into branching transport networks that contract over time toward efficient connectivity between food sources. It is the same positive-feedback mechanism as ant pheromone trails, and it reproduces the real *Physarum polycephalum* experiments in which the organism approximates rail networks. In generative art it is prized because the output is genuinely emergent and never repeats, and because the three parameters — sensor angle, sensor distance, decay rate — produce dramatically different network morphologies.
algorithms.citation: Jones, Characteristics of Pattern Formation and Evolution in Approximations of Physarum Transport Networks, Artificial Life 16(2), 127–153

algorithms.name: FABRIK
algorithms.summary: Solves inverse kinematics by moving points along lines instead of solving for angles. Fast, stable, and visually natural.
algorithms.eli5: Forget angles altogether and treat the limb as beads on a string. Drag the hand bead onto the target, then walk back along the string putting each bead at the correct distance from the one after it. Then sweep the other way to put the shoulder back where it belongs. Two sweeps, and it looks natural.
algorithms.description: Forward And Backward Reaching Inverse Kinematics works entirely in positions and never builds a Jacobian. The backward pass moves the end effector onto the target, then walks down the chain: each joint is repositioned onto the line joining it to the joint after it, at exactly its bone length away. That satisfies every length constraint but has now dragged the root off its anchor. The forward pass puts the root back and repeats the same procedure outward. Iterate until the end effector is close enough. Because each step is a point-on-a-line calculation there are no matrix inverses, no singularities, and no oscillation near full extension — the failure modes that make Jacobian solvers unpleasant. Joint limits are applied by clamping each repositioned joint into its allowed cone before continuing.
algorithms.citation: FABRIK: A fast, iterative solver for the Inverse Kinematics problem, Graphical Models 73(5), 243–260

algorithms.name: Novelty search
algorithms.summary: Abandon the objective entirely and reward behavioural difference from everything seen before.
algorithms.eli5: Stop scoring attempts on how good they are and score them on how *unlike* everything you have already seen they are. Counter-intuitively this often reaches the goal sooner, because the obvious score marches you confidently up a hill that turns out to be the wrong hill.
algorithms.description: Replace the fitness function with a novelty measure: score each individual by how far its *behaviour* is from its nearest neighbours in an archive of previously seen behaviours, and add anything sufficiently novel to that archive. Nothing rewards being good at the task. The argument is that ambitious objectives are deceptive — the gradient toward them usually leads into dead ends, because the stepping stones to a hard goal rarely look like progress toward it. Rewarding novelty instead keeps expanding the frontier of what has been tried, and on deceptive problems this reliably beats objective-driven search at reaching the objective. For content generation the relevance is direct: you usually want a diverse set of interesting artefacts, not one optimum, and this is the first method that treats diversity as the goal rather than as a means.
